content: An epicanthal fold, also known as an epicanthic fold or epicanthus, is a fold of skin on the upper eyelid that extends from the nose to the inner side of the eyebrow, covering the inner corner (medial canthus) of the eye. This anatomical feature is commonly observed in individuals of East Asian descent, including populations such as Mongols, Turks, Chinese, Koreans, Japanese, Vietnamese, and other ethnic groups from East and Southeast Asia, such as Indonesians and Malaysians. It is also present in Inuit populations, some Indian groups, and the Khoisan people of Africa and Madagascar. In young children of any ethnicity, epicanthal folds may be present before the nasal bridge develops and elevates. The term epicanthal fold is a descriptive term based on appearance, but the physiological reasons for its presence can vary significantly between individuals. During fetal development, all humans initially form epicanthal folds. While some children lose these folds before birth, others retain them during early childhood, regardless of ethnicity, until the nasal bridge elevates. In cases of preterm birth or maternal alcohol consumption during pregnancy, epicanthal folds may persist. In children, the presence of epicanthal folds can sometimes create the appearance of crossed eyes, a condition referred to as pseudostrabismus. In individuals of Caucasian or other ethnic backgrounds where epicanthal folds are not typically present, their occurrence can be associated with certain pathological conditions. These include fetal alcohol syndrome, chromosomal abnormalities such as Down syndrome (Trisomy 21), Cri du Chat syndrome, or preterm birth. The epicanthal fold is a hereditary trait in many populations worldwide. While it is absent in some groups, it is prevalent among many East Asian and Southeast Asian populations. It is also found in significant numbers among Native Americans, the Khoisan people of Southern Africa, Central Asians, and some individuals of Sami origin. Additionally, it is common in people of Tibetan descent, including Tibetans and certain North-East Burmese populations. Due to genetic inheritance, children born to one parent with a pronounced epicanthal fold and another without it may exhibit varying degrees of epicanthal folds. In East Asian populations, the presence of an epicanthal fold is often associated with a less prominent upper eyelid crease, commonly referred to as single eyelids, in contrast to double eyelids. However, the epicanthal fold and the upper eyelid crease are distinct features, and an individual may have one, both, or neither. The surgical procedure to reduce or remove epicanthal folds is known as epicanthoplasty. This procedure is now rarely performed. However, Asian blepharoplasty, a cosmetic surgery aimed at creating a more prominent upper eyelid crease, remains a popular procedure in East Asia.
